title: Indian Hills
text:
Three years after the marriage and two children later, we were looking for our first home.
Two houses were available, same price, close to each other, same school district with one significant difference.
One was facing a busy street and the other was in a neighborhood-only road.
We weren’t sure since we were new to house hunting.
My mother said,

“Look towards the future when your children are toddlers, would you want them to ride their tricycles near a busy road.”

That sealed our decision to move into the Indian Hills area of the town.

The lot south of the new house was empty and was kept that way by the neighbor across from us.
He wanted an unencumbered view of Utah Lake.
Often he would battle the weeds, especially dandelions on the .22 acre (9583 square feet) plot.
For our children and the neighbor’s grandson, the empty lot was their playground that was larger than their imagination.

It was at that house 2 more children joined the family.
As my mom predicted our children learned how to ride tricycles and bicycles on the driveway and on the road by the house.
Later on we learned that the neighbor across the street was at one time a high profile corporate lawyer that worked for what was then the largest corporation in the world.
We sold the house when the work assigned me to work overseas.
We had realized a sizeable return on investment but most of all because we listened to a more wise voice, we were able to raise the family in relative peace and quiet.

title: Knight Block Winterization
text:
Ryan from Told Plumbing along with Greg representing REMS Corp. met in the basement of the Knight Building, located at 1 East Center Street, Provo, on the morning or 6 October 2026
The main purpose of the gathering was to winterize the building by turning on the main boiler than services nearly 20,000 square feet of office and restaurant spaces.
The unit was manufactured in 1990 and once a year, a technician initiated a set of sequences that heated water to 180 degrees farenheit and pumped the water to each spaces in the building.
In turn each space or office had a controller that pulled in heated water to create the radiant heat, the old, yet efficient heating method

The boiler consist of 3 separate systems, water circulation, gas heating and electrical ignition and control
The water circulation was controlled at 35 to 65 psi.
The heated water is pulled to each floor using an in-line pump.
When the water releases its heat the water is returned to the boiler to be re-heated.
It is a closed loop system.
Gas provides the energy to increase the water temperature from room temperature, 80 to 90 degrees up to 170 to 180 degree farenheit.
This heating up takes nearly 2 days and the cooling down takes equally long.
The gas system is similar to home heating, except there is a danger of too much pressure buildup.
There is a pressure sensor and a relief valve that opens to release the water to bring the pressure back down.
The water temperature is set by a limit switch. Turning on the gas heating when the water temperature falls below a certain value.

After the boiler introduction, Greg took us up to the attic to show us the glycerin based fire suppression,
The clock tower has no insulation and is exposed to elements. The inside temperature would be few degrees higher than outside temperature during winter.
Glycerin freezes at 0 degrees farenheit.
He showed us 3 AHU, air handling units.
North, Middle and South.
He thought one of the 3rd floor units would be replaced.
We thought one of the 2nd floor units was to be replaced next spring.

title: Matrix Adventure
text:
The 13-hour flight was beginning to feel like a full day’s journey.
Fighting a 180 mph headwind, it was as if we were treading water, 38,000 feet above the Pacific Ocean, suspended somewhere near the International Date Line.
Desperate for a distraction to make the time pass faster, I opened the in-flight entertainment system, and began browsing the movie selection.
I scrolled over to a category labeled Critically Acclaimed.
Almost every title was like a new release to me since I had suspended watching movies and television series back in the mid-1990s, leaving a considerable gap in my pop culture knowledge.
As I browsed, a series of titles stood out — The Matrix.
I had heard people talk about this film for decades, but I had never actually seen it for myself.

I settled on the first in the series, released in 1999.
At two hours and sixteen minutes, it seemed like an ideal distraction du jour for a long journey.
However, the initial pacing of the movie mirrored our flight—methodical and slow to build.
I was expecting a story with a well defined protagonist whose path follows Joseph Campbell’s Hero’s Journey.
But for the first half of the film, no such figure—or pattern—emerged.
Out of boredom and frustration, I switched my monitor back to the flight tracking map.
At least the flight data gave me a sense of progression, showing a quantifiable distance closing toward our destination.
Then, the story and the flight progression converged.

As our plane skirted the Kamchatka Peninsula and crossed the Sea of Okhotsk, the heavy headwinds finally eased.
The aircraft picked up speed, cruising steadily toward its destination.
The narrative revealed its reluctant hero, along with the allies who helped him recognize his purpose.
Neo discovered a singular mission: to rescue his captured mentor, Morpheus.
Armed with his new training and supported by Trinity, Neo stepped into his true identity, overcoming his nemesis Agent Smith and the simulated system built to hold humanity back.
Watching this ordinary man awaken to his purpose in life reminded me of the core message in Viktor Frankl’s Man’s Search for Meaning:

“It did not really matter what we expected from life, but rather what life expected from us.”

Frankl taught that we must stop asking about the meaning of life in the abstract. Instead, we must recognize that life questions us—and we answer through our actions, our choices, and how we meet our daily responsibilities.
Viktor Frankl learned this in the concentration camps; Neo learned it inside the artificial reality of the Matrix.
Likewise, we discover meaning not by waiting for ideal circumstances, but by accepting our responsibilities, refining our choices, and recognizing that each of us has a unique mission—one that continually unfolds over time.
As Ellie so enthusiastically declared from Charles Muntz’s motto in Up!:

“Adventure is out there!”

title: Family Gathering
text:
Returning from a western city road trip follows a unwritten script: minimum pit stops and pack some snacks in order to get home as fast as legally possible.
We seldom consider sitting down for a meal, since that would negate the minutes saved traveling at allowable speeds—hence the importance of snacks consumed in the car.
On this particular visit, we decided to join the group just two days before the event.
Because of the short planning horizon, we weren’t even at our destination for twenty-four hours, and we didn’t plan any sightseeing.
The mission of this trip was simple: to get better acquainted with the children of our nieces and nephews—kids we seldom see, let alone interact with.

A Setting Built for Connection
Staying at a hotel is convenient but it isolates families into separate rooms, but choosing a short-term rental proved to be the right choice.
The layout was built for interactions: three bedrooms on the west side, four more on the east, with common areas; kitchen, dining and family rooms. And all thirteen beds would be occupied by the visiting groups.
In total, there were ten children under one roof, ranging in age from nine down to one, with clusters at ages six and four.
Watching them interact was a reminder in human nature.
The children knew how to associate instinctively—falling into games, laughter, and shared spaces without hesitation or awkwardness.
The adults, on the other hand, had to relearn how to do it.
We were busy getting involved in a shared game room, an outdoor pool, and a bubbling hot tub.
It provided the grown-ups a chance to learn again how to be around children at play.


The Cost of Gathering
Even in a city as large and diverse as Las Vegas, securing a reservation for thirty people was a challenge.
We were told to confirm our table an hour before arrival, only to be reminded of a spending minimum upon calling.
When we finally arrived, we were asked to wait twenty minutes—which stretched closer to an hour before we finally tasted some food.
Yet, once the food began to flow, it was exceptional.
Enhanced by the atmosphere created by the arrangement of children seated in bench seats into their newly formed groups, facing their parents.
With the grandparents in the middle section of the room, flanked by 2 tables with grandchildren.
When the check arrived, it rivaled the cost of the last used car I purchased. I didn’t feel the price was high.
More importantly, we had gathered in one place to reaffirm our bonds as descendants of our parents.


The Road Home
The next morning brought a slow, family by family checkout process, each leaving for their next destination.
Someone had ordered bagels and cream cheese for a light send-off.
With no more plans left, we waited until everyone else had departed, locked the front door, and hit the road.
We planned our pit stops and estimated our arrival time at home as we pulled out of Clark County.
But then, after two and a half hours of driving—just as we passed Cedar City near mile marker 37—we received a phone call from a group that had left hours before us.
They told us they were waiting at a rest stop about thirty minutes ahead. Furthermore, they had stopped by a Korean market along the way.






As we were getting hungry, it was the most welcome message imaginable.
It was the fourth daughter and her husband, thoughtfully looking out for the second and third daughters and their husbands.
They were standing outside, waving as we pulled into the rest stop.
All the Korean favorites were laid out: 떡, 김밥, katsu, and pastries.
We hadn’t planned to eat like this, and we certainly weren’t expecting it.
However, there along the I-15, between mile markers 87 and 88, we were fed with food that we had grown up with.
This weekend I felt the importance of gathering of family members.
The continuation and confirmation of linkage between generations.
Both the family you are born into and the family you marry into.

title: Clear and Present Goal
text:
During the years working with the young adults, we went camping regularly.
It wasn’t because it was a crowd favorite, nor was it the most convenient thing to organize.
We did it because of a conversation with another leader at a backyard wedding reception.
The newlyweds were using their leader’s home as the venue.
The property was located in the Tree Streets neighborhood, framed by mature trees and a gently sloped yard that drifted from east to west. As the evening wore on and the celebration settled, I found the homeowner and began comparing notes.
Foremost on my mind as a new leader was a simple question:

How do you bring young people together in a way that allows genuine courtships to form and lead to marriage?

He smiled and shared that his unit held dozens of weddings the past year.
I was all ears.


He shared their secret: they went camping as a group.
For reasons he couldn’t fully articulate, nature seemed to break down barriers, allowing young people to get acquainted almost effortlessly.
He didn’t need to elaborate—the results he quoted were enough for me.
Inspired by his advice, I began searching for campsites that fit a set of constraints:

Accessibility: The campsite had to be within a one-hour drive of our home base.
Co-ed Accommodations: The location needed to safely and comfortably host both young men and women in the same general area.

In the end, three locations met our criteria.
One was a traditional outdoor campsite, while the other two offered a hybrid experience with the comfort of indoor plumbing and sleeping facilities.
With our venues selected, we were ready to put his theory to the test.

text:
On a recent return trip, see link, we talked about food we grew up with.
We talked about regional differences.
Somehow we dialed in on kimchi.
Winter kimchi at that.
I recall mom orchestrating a dozen or so ladies in annual winterization effort, ensuring that our family will have “fresh” vegetables during dormant winter months.
The prepared kimchi, would be placed inside 항아리, which were then buried under groun
Then during the winter days, when grounds were frozen, these nearly frozen kimchi provided the necessary nutrients.
Particularly memorable were those radishes which were salted or pickled.

Advancements in both a year round farming, nationwide logistics, and mass scale kimchi making eliminated the need for private kimchi making along with any regional differences.

title: Where Your Heart
text:
During scouting trips to Heber City, met a couple serving in Lake Creek Campground.
They had brought a camper that was parked at the entrance. That camper served as their home while they served on the church mission.
They commented that when couples retire they purchase grown up toys and those toys require their time. Thus few couples serve a mission.
Where your treasure is there will be your heart.

Recognized a person during a visit to 1400 South 1100 West Orem
His parents lived in our Ward, 8th, and he built his house just south of it, within 5th Ward boundary.
He mentioned that his mother was still alive and living in the home.
Asked how many mission they served
Seven.
We know of a couple, Geertsens that served 8 missions.
Where were their hearts, where were there treasures.

title: Ginko Tree
text:
참으로 오랜만이었네.
천 년을 사는 은행나무는 몇십 년에 한 번씩 봐도 되지만,
백 년도 못 사는 사람은 몇 년에 한 번이라도 보고 사는 게 친척 아니겠나.
반가웠고 잘 살아줘서 고맙네. 어디에 얼마나 멀리 살아도 늘 기억하고 추억하며 열심히 살고 건강하세.
It really had been such a long time!
The ginkgo tree, which lives a thousand years, can be seen once every few decades and still be fine.
But people, who don’t even live a hundred years, should see each other at least once every few years—that’s what being relatives is all about.
It was so good to see you, and thank you for living well.
No matter where we live or how far apart we may be, let’s remember each other, cherish our memories, keep working hard, and stay healthy.
Uncle Hong, October 2026


In life there are at least 2 families
The family that you are born into and the family that you become through marriage.
By marrying Sister K, I became acquainted with her eight aunts and two uncles.
One uncle is older than Sister K’s father by a few years.
But the younger uncle is nearly 20 years younger.
We made arrangements to visit him and his new wife.
He suggested instead of visiting for a dinner, we should come earlier and he will show around the town,
